_meta.purpose: STOF Default Configuration Check Knowledge Base -- real disclosed bug bounty patterns for stof/modules/configuration_tests.py.
sources: PortSwigger Research -- 'Exploiting CORS misconfigurations for Bitcoins and bounties' (canonical methodology reference)
PortSwigger Web Security Academy -- 'CORS vulnerability with basic origin reflection' lab
HackerOne #426165 (Zomato) -- Origin header reflected verbatim into Access-Control-Allow-Origin
HackerOne #1194280 (Sifchain) -- Access-Control-Allow-Origin dynamically echoes client Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
HackerOne #470298 (U.S. DoD) -- same reflected-origin + credentials pattern, publicly disclosed
_meta.key_finding: configuration_tests.py already covers 5 well-known default-configuration exposure classes (admin panels, directory listing, debug-mode stack traces, sample/install files, version-disclosure headers) via curated path/header lists. The clearest remaining real-world gap is CORS misconfiguration: a server that dynamically reflects an arbitrary attacker-supplied Origin header back into Access-Control-Allow-Origin AND sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true -- letting any attacker-controlled website read a victim's authenticated API responses cross-origin. This is one of the most frequently disclosed HackerOne misconfiguration classes, with a precise, narrow evidence bar that avoids a very common false-positive trap: a static Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with no (or false) Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is NOT exploitable for authenticated requests (browsers reject the */credentials combo outright) and must not be flagged. An HTTP-methods-enabled-via-OPTIONS candidate was also researched but had materially weaker disclosed-report evidence (usually cited alongside a real PUT/DELETE exploitation writeup, not as a standalone header-inspection bounty) -- not built this wave, consistent with this project's real-disclosed-evidence-only bar. CSP analysis (TC-017.7) closes a second identified gap, LIVE-CONFIRMED FAILING against demo.testfire.net -- the target's root HTML response carries no Content-Security-Policy header at all.
csp_weakness_sources: PortSwigger 'CSP allows untrusted script execution' advisory -- unsafe-inline/unsafe-eval/wildcard-source weaknesses
Google Strict CSP methodology -- what a genuinely strict policy looks like, including the nonce-/hash-plus-unsafe-inline backward-compat pattern
HackerOne #225833 -- a real, disclosed CSP-gap report, low-severity precisely because it lacked an actual XSS to chain with
_meta.wave_2_key_finding: Four candidates researched this wave: security-header hygiene (clickjacking/MIME-sniffing), TLS/transport analysis, HTTP-method (OPTIONS/Allow) enumeration, and public cloud-storage exposure. Three held up to this project's real-disclosed-evidence bar and were built as TC-017.8/9/10, reusing configuration_tests.py's existing single-response header-inspection and _probe_get patterns -- no new probing mechanism was needed. The fourth, HTTP-method analysis, was re-verified with fresh research (OWASP WSTG 'Test HTTP Methods', and current bug-bounty write-ups) and still does not clear the bar as a standalone finding -- see http_method_analysis_not_built below for the specific reasoning, unchanged in substance from the wave-1 conclusion already recorded in this file's original key_finding.
wave_2_sources: OWASP Secure Headers Project -- 'core' recommended response header set (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies); MDN's own note that CSP's frame-ancestors directive supersedes X-Frame-Options in every browser that implements it
OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet -- HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options guidance
OWASP WSTG -- 'Test HTTP Methods' (04-...-06) -- current authoritative methodology for the HTTP-method-enumeration technique that was researched and not built

HackerOne disclosed reports on public S3 bucket listing/exposure as a recurring, well-documented class: reports #1173598 (U.S. DoD -- S3 bucket listing, full download), #3382796 (AWS VDP -- publicly listable/readable bucket exposing JSON/config files), #819278 (Greenhouse.io -- open S3 bucket, no auth, directory navigation and download), #278191 (X/xAI -- listable S3 bucket), #209223 and #194142 (Ruby, Legal Robot -- open/writeable S3 buckets)

patterns.generalized_transformation: Send a GET request to an authenticated/API-shaped endpoint carrying a clearly non-allowlisted, attacker-controlled `Origin` header (e.g. `https://stof-cors-probe.invalid`). Inspect ONLY the response headers -- no state change, no authentication even required to demonstrate the misconfiguration on a public endpoint (a real attack additionally relies on the victim's browser attaching real session cookies, which STOF doesn't need to simulate to prove the server-side reflection behavior itself).
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any discovered endpoint, preferably `endpoint_type == "api"`, that echoes CORS headers at all -- falls back to the target's base URL if no API endpoint was discovered.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern_note: Same origin-relative probing style as the module's existing `_probe_paths`.
patterns.evidence_signal: BOTH conditions must hold together, not either alone: (1) the response's `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` value is EXACTLY the attacker-supplied Origin string sent (proving dynamic reflection, not a static allowlist entry or wildcard) AND (2) `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` is present and literally `true` in the same response. A static `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with no/false Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is explicitly NOT a hit -- must be excluded, this is the documented common false-positive trap.
patterns.real_example: Zomato (HackerOne #426165) -- Origin `developersxzomato.com` reflected verbatim into ACAO; Sifchain (HackerOne #1194280) -- ACAO dynamically echoes client Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true; U.S. DoD VDP (HackerOne #470298) -- same reflected-origin + credentials pattern.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as configuration_tests.py's _technique_cors_misconfiguration: one anonymous-context GET, header `Origin: https://stof-cors-probe.invalid`, sent to the first discovered endpoint_type=="api" endpoint (else falls back to _target_url, same fallback convention as every other TC-017 technique). Access-Control-Allow-Origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials are read case-insensitively and passed to a pure, directly-unit-tested helper, _is_cors_misconfigured(sent_origin, acao, acac) -> bool, which FAILs only when ACAO exactly equals the sent Origin string AND ACAC is present and literally "true" -- unit-tested against all 4 boolean combinations (reflected+true -> True; reflected+missing -> False; wildcard '*'+true -> False; non-reflecting static origin+true -> False), so the documented false-positive trap (a static ACAO: * with no/false ACAC) is provably never flagged. A network failure on the probe itself returns ERROR (not a silent PASS), matching _technique_version_disclosure's own except-block pattern. Real-world validation: run against demo.testfire.net (2026-08-26) -- result PASS, ACAO was not reflected back for the synthetic Origin (the target's only concurrent TC-017 finding that run was TC-017.5, an unrelated Apache-Coyote/1.1 version-disclosure header). A clean PASS here is the expected, legitimate outcome for a target without this misconfiguration, not a gap in the check.

patterns.generalized_transformation: A single anonymous-context GET to the target's base URL, header inspection only -- no wordlist sweep, same shape as _technique_version_disclosure. Only runs against a `text/html` response (a missing CSP on a JSON/API/static-asset response is normal, not a finding). Checks, in order: no CSP header present at all; `unsafe-inline` in the effective script directive WITHOUT a `nonce-`/`hash-` source also present in that same directive (the real, still-strict-for-modern-browsers backward-compat pattern -- must not be flagged); `unsafe-eval` present; a bare `*`, `data:`, or bare `https:` scheme source. A strict `default-src 'self'` policy with none of those keywords is never flagged just for being short.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: The target's base URL (_target_url), same fallback convention as every other TC-017 technique -- a defense-in-depth header check applies to the site's own root response, not a specific discovered endpoint.
patterns.evidence_signal: Content-Type is text/html AND (no Content-Security-Policy header at all, OR the effective script-src/default-src directive carries unsafe-inline without a nonce/hash, unsafe-eval, or an overly broad source keyword).
patterns.real_example: HackerOne #225833 -- a real, disclosed CSP-gap report, explicitly low-severity because it lacked an actual XSS injection point to chain the missing CSP protection against; the finding here is deliberately worded the same way (defense-in-depth gap, not a confirmed exploit path on its own).

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as configuration_tests.py's _technique_csp_weakness plus a pure, directly-unit-tested helper _csp_missing_or_weak(content_type, csp_header) -> str | None. The helper does a small split-on-';'/whitespace directive parse (no full CSP grammar) and inspects only script-src, falling back to default-src when script-src is absent, per the CSP spec's own directive-fallback behavior. Unit-tested against every false-positive guard from the research: non-HTML content-type -> None; missing header on HTML -> hit; unsafe-inline alone -> hit; unsafe-inline plus a nonce/hash source in the same directive -> None (the guard); unsafe-eval -> hit; bare */data:/https: source -> hit; a strict default-src 'self' policy -> None; script-src present overrides a weak default-src. Severity is Medium per the research's own HackerOne #225833 precedent, and the Finding description states this is a defense-in-depth gap, not a confirmed exploit path, honestly. Real-world validation: run against demo.testfire.net (2026-08-27, scan_45f2c657) -- result FAIL: the root response (Content-Type: text/html;charset=ISO-8859-1) carries no Content-Security-Policy header at all, the simplest of the three checks the helper covers. allow_state_changing_probes remained false/untouched for this run (this technique never gates on it).

patterns.generalized_transformation: The exact same single anonymous-context GET to the target's base URL that _technique_version_disclosure and _technique_csp_weakness already issue -- no new probe. Only runs against a text/html response. Checks X-Content-Type-Options is exactly 'nosniff' and that a clickjacking control exists (X-Frame-Options present, OR the response's CSP carries a frame-ancestors directive).
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: The target's base URL (_target_url), same fallback convention as every other TC-017 technique.
patterns.evidence_signal: Content-Type is text/html AND (X-Content-Type-Options is absent or not literally 'nosniff', OR both X-Frame-Options is absent AND no frame-ancestors CSP directive is present). Named per-header in the finding description so a pentester knows exactly which control is missing, not a generic 'headers missing'.
patterns.false_positive_guard: CSP's frame-ancestors directive supersedes X-Frame-Options in every browser that implements it (OWASP Secure Headers Project / MDN) -- a response with only frame-ancestors set is NOT flagged for a missing X-Frame-Options, which would otherwise double-count the same clickjacking control STOF's own TC-017.7 CSP check already partially inspects.
patterns.real_example: OWASP Secure Headers Project's 'core' recommended set and OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet -- these two headers are the narrow, genuinely security-relevant subset (clickjacking + MIME-sniffing) distinct from HSTS, which TC-017.9 owns as a transport-security concern rather than a generic header-hygiene one.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as configuration_tests.py's _technique_missing_security_headers plus a pure, directly-unit-tested helper _missing_security_headers(content_type, headers) -> list[str]. Unit-tested against: both headers absent -> both named; both present -> []; frame-ancestors present without X-Frame-Options -> [] (the guard); non-HTML content-type -> []; X-Content-Type-Options present but not literally 'nosniff' -> flagged. Real-world validation: run against demo.testfire.net (2026-08-27, scan_f9616385) -- result FAIL: the root text/html response is missing both X-Content-Type-Options and X-Frame-Options. allow_state_changing_probes remained false/untouched for this run.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Two-part check, scoped to what a single Playwright HTTP GET can honestly establish (no raw-socket/OpenSSL cipher-suite audit -- that needs a socket-level tool, not context.request.*): (1) any discovered endpoint whose URL path looks credential/session/payment-shaped (login, signin, auth, password, account, session, checkout, payment, billing, token) AND is reachable over plain http:// with a non-error status; (2) if the target itself is HTTPS and no such plaintext-sensitive endpoint exists, a GET to the target checking whether Strict-Transport-Security is present.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Discovered endpoints (_sensitive_http_endpoints) for the plaintext check; the target's base URL (_target_url) for the HSTS check -- same fallback convention as every other TC-017 technique.
patterns.evidence_signal: EITHER a sensitive-shaped endpoint answers over http:// with status < 400 (Critical -- credentials/tokens interceptable in transit) OR the HTTPS target sends no Strict-Transport-Security header at all (Low -- SSL-stripping downgrade risk on a future plaintext visit, not an active compromise).
patterns.false_positive_guard: A non-sensitive path (a static asset, a public marketing page) served over plain HTTP is explicitly not flagged -- only the narrow keyword-matched sensitive-path set triggers the Critical plaintext-transport finding, avoiding flagging every http:// asset URL a mixed-content page might reference.
patterns.real_example: General TLS/transport-security best-practice consensus (OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet's HSTS section) rather than a single bounty report -- this is deliberately the narrower, honestly-scoped half of 'TLS configuration analysis': a genuine cipher-suite/protocol-version audit needs a raw socket, which is out of scope for this technique per the task's own instruction.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as configuration_tests.py's _technique_tls_configuration, reusing the existing _probe_get helper for the sensitive-endpoint sweep (transient errors still propagate the same way every other technique in this file handles them) and the module's now-familiar single-header-GET shape for the HSTS check. Unit-tested: sensitive http:// endpoint reachable -> FAIL; non-sensitive http:// endpoint (e.g. a .png asset) -> PASS (the guard); HTTPS target missing HSTS -> FAIL; HTTPS target with HSTS -> PASS. Real-world validation: run against demo.testfire.net (2026-08-27, scan_f9616385) -- result FAIL: the target is HTTPS but sends no Strict-Transport-Security header; no discovered endpoint matched the sensitive-path keyword set over plaintext HTTP in this run. allow_state_changing_probes remained false/untouched.

patterns.generalized_transformation: NOT BUILT. An OPTIONS request to a sensitive/discovered endpoint, checking whether the Allow or Access-Control-Allow-Methods response header advertises PUT/DELETE/TRACE beyond the application's actual discovered GET/POST surface.
patterns.why_not_built: Re-verified this wave with fresh research (OWASP WSTG 'Test HTTP Methods', current 2026 bug-bounty methodology write-ups) and the conclusion from wave 1 still holds: an Allow-header listing PUT/DELETE is not reliable standalone evidence of exploitability. Frameworks routinely advertise methods in Allow/OPTIONS that the actual route handler still rejects (405/501) when invoked for real -- the header reflects what the router *could* dispatch, not what the handler *implements*. Every disclosed report actually citing method-based findings pairs it with a real PUT/DELETE/TRACE invocation that changed or deleted server state or reflected the request (e.g. an actual successful file upload via PUT, not just PUT appearing in Allow) -- exactly the 'weaker -- usually cited alongside a real PUT/DELETE exploitation writeup, not a standalone header-inspection bounty' caveat this project already flagged. Building a header-only version here would produce a technique whose FAIL is frequently a false positive relative to real exploitability, which fails this project's evidence-bar discipline (see stof-enterprise-dev skill: 'a false positive wastes a pentester's day'). A future PUT/DELETE technique that actually attempts (and verifies via response-body signature, not status-code-alone) a real state-changing write would be the honestly-buildable version of this idea, but that requires allow_state_changing_probes=true gating and is a materially different, larger technique than a passive OPTIONS/Allow header check -- out of scope for this wave's read-only-probe instruction.

stof_coverage.notes: Deliberately not implemented -- see why_not_built. No TC-017.x number was reserved for it.

patterns.generalized_transformation: A single GET to the target's base URL, scan the HTML/JS response body for cloud-storage-shaped URLs via a small regex list (S3 virtual-hosted and path-style, Azure Blob, GCS), cap at 5 distinct candidates. For each candidate, one follow-up GET; a hit requires the response body to carry an actual object-listing root-element signature (<ListBucketResult for S3/GCS XML API, <EnumerationResults for Azure), never status code or bucket-name pattern alone -- an AccessDenied/NoSuchBucket/ContainerNotFound error response uses a completely different XML root element, so a locked-down bucket can never be confused with an open one.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: The target's base URL response body is the source of candidate storage URLs (_find_cloud_storage_urls); each candidate URL is then probed directly via _probe_get, same transient-error handling as every other probe in this file.
patterns.evidence_signal: A referenced storage URL's response body contains a bucket/container-listing root element (<ListBucketResult or <EnumerationResults). Absence of any referenced storage URL, or a listing-signature-free response (including any error body), is PASS.
patterns.real_example: A well-documented, recurring HackerOne finding class across many programs: #1173598 (U.S. DoD -- S3 bucket listing and full download), #3382796 (AWS VDP -- publicly listable/readable bucket exposing JSON/config files used in production), #819278 (Greenhouse.io -- open S3 bucket, directory navigation and download, no auth required), #278191 (X/xAI -- listable S3 bucket via AWS CLI), #209223 (Ruby -- open/writeable S3 bucket), #194142 (Legal Robot -- AWS S3 bucket information disclosure).

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as configuration_tests.py's _technique_cloud_storage_exposure plus two pure, directly-unit-tested helpers: _find_cloud_storage_urls(body) -> list[str] (dedup, order-preserving, capped at 5) and _is_bucket_listing(body) -> bool (checks only the listing-signature strings, never a status code). Unit-tested: no URLs referenced -> PASS; a referenced bucket returning a real <ListBucketResult> listing -> FAIL; a referenced bucket returning an AccessDenied/NoSuchBucket <Error> body -> PASS (the guard, proving the check can't be fooled by a bucket merely existing and being referenced). Real-world validation: run against demo.testfire.net (2026-08-27, scan_f9616385) -- result PASS: the target's HTML referenced no S3/Azure Blob/GCS-shaped URLs to check, the expected clean outcome for a target with no cloud-storage references at all, not a gap in the check. allow_state_changing_probes remained false/untouched -- this technique is GET-only throughout.
